newsitem.title: KENYA: Corruption, security seen threat to Kenyan future.
newsitem.headline: Corruption, security seen threat to Kenyan future.

text.p: A rise in violent crime and rampant official corruption ahead of Kenya's general elections are undermining four years of economic reforms, diplomats and financial leaders say.
They say with elections next year Kenya has the chance to show the world its commitment to economic reforms was a political reality. But this meant tackling crime and the scourge of corruption.

Kenya has forecast gross domestic product (GDP) growth at 6.0 percent in 1996. But economic analysts say a slower process of privatisations, low tea prices and security jitters threaten new investment.

"The challenges Kenya faces are substantial. Continuing with economic reforms to promote an enabling environment for trade and development will take courage and sacrifice," U.S. Ambassador Prudence Bushnell told a meeting on Thursday night.
"Zero tolerance for corruption is hard to implement...but zero tolerance is indispensable to economic growth," she added.
"Nothing undermines issues and investor confidence so much as unchecked corruption; it needs to be cut back forcefully."
Bushnell and Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi have in recent days spoken out against rising violent crime and Moi has ordered his police to strike harder at criminals to restore order.
"It is clear that there are some criminal-minded people who imagine that they can rob banks and take other people's property by force and get away with it," Moi said in a speech last week.

Responding to a tour operator who complained that a slowdown in tourist traffic from America because of security problems had severely hurt the industry, Bushnell said: "I cannot pretend that crime has gone down. There is still insecurity in Kenya."
Kenya's parliament debated growing insecurity on Thursday and a legislator from the ruling KANU party said he had evidence that a police officer was involved in cattle rustling.
Vice-President George Saitoti told parliament that crime was adversely affecting the economy and could deter investors.
Last week heavily-armed gangsters launched two daring raids in Nairobi's city centre, leading East Africa's leading paper, The Daily Nation, to warn of impending chaos in stable Kenya.
On Friday, Nairobi's East African Standard newspaper reported that police gunned down two gangsters and wounded two others after they had hijacked a car on a Nairobi street on Thursday.
Kenya's police chief says police will restore order.
Police have detained as many as 400 people in the last two weeks and have paraded before television cameras four people they said were criminals involved in robbery and carjackings.
Kenya's next general election will be held next year and Moi said last week he would defend the presidency. The opposition is deeply divided and an easy Moi victory is widely expected.
Finance Minister Musalia Mudavadi says liberalisation measures mean that avenues for corruption have been reduced and more reforms and discipline will cut graft further.
Brokers at the Nairobi Stock Exchange say one reason why the market has been depressed for months is the perception that Kenyan leaders were not doing enough to stamp out crime.
"Investors love a secure environment, here there is this feeling that not enough is done for this," one broker said.

Business leaders fear events could go the way of 1992 when Kenya held landmark pluralist elections. Then violence rocked parts of the country in the runup to the poll and killed up to 1,000 people and made 250,000 homeless, U.N. officials say.
